title: MEL ONE — Timber Notes
description: Plain-language guides to planning, materials and timber work — prepared to help you ask better questions before work begins.

items.title: Carpenter, joiner or cabinet maker: who does your project need?
items.summary: Choose the right timber scope and agree the handovers between site carpentry, architectural joinery and cabinetry before comparing quotes.
items.content_text:
Choose by the work and its interfaces: a carpenter handles site timber work, a joiner creates fitted timber details, and a cabinet maker focuses on cabinets and storage. The scope can overlap, so confirm each provider’s actual responsibilities.

Start with the object and the stage of work: Site carpentry may involve framing, doors, trims or renovation timber work. Architectural joinery involves fitted features and detailed timber elements; cabinet making focuses on kitchens, wardrobes and other storage. These descriptions are a starting point, not proof of a provider’s capability. List the items you need and ask who will measure, manufacture, install and finish each one.

Coordination is a responsibility to agree: One contact can make communication simpler, but a combined quote does not establish that every trade is delivered by the same person. Ask which work is included, which specialists are separately engaged and who resolves the junctions. A clear allocation of responsibilities matters whether you appoint one provider or several.

Check evidence against the proposed work: Ask for relevant work examples and a written description of the proposed scope. Confirm who contracts the work, who supervises it where required and how to check the relevant licence details. A workshop, a broad service list or a company registration alone does not establish authority for every type of building work.

Where coordination usually breaks down: The high-risk moments are rarely dramatic: a wall is lined before a niche is measured, a benchtop is ordered before services are set, or a door swing conflicts with a cabinet installed later. These gaps occur when each trade works from a different assumption. A coordinated carpentry and joinery process makes the interfaces visible before they become site fixes.

One measure does not mean one guess: Integrated delivery is not about taking a single measurement and hoping it survives the build. It means revisiting critical dimensions at the right stage, documenting changes and deciding when workshop production should begin. Site conditions, linings, floor finishes and services can all affect the final fit, so the sequence matters as much as the initial design.

How to compare scopes, not just totals: When comparing quotes, look for who owns set-out, site measure, shop drawings, material selection, protection, installation, adjustments and handover. A low initial figure may exclude the coordination that makes a complex room fit together. A useful quote names assumptions and interfaces so the owner can see what must be resolved before work starts.

A practical project workflow: For a renovation or new build, the process normally moves from brief and drawings to site verification, detail decisions, production timing, staged installation and final adjustment. Not every project needs a large formal programme, but every project benefits from agreeing who makes decisions, when dimensions are confirmed and how late changes will be managed.

Questions to ask before appointing a team: Ask what work is completed in-house, who will be your site contact, how measurements are verified, when custom pieces are released for manufacture and how defects or changes are handled. Clear answers demonstrate process knowledge. They are more informative than broad claims about quality because they show how a team protects quality under real project conditions.

items.title: Kitchen cabinetry costs: how to compare an Adelaide quote
items.summary: Understand the cabinetry choices, site work, allowances and exclusions that shape a kitchen quote, without relying on generic market price bands.
items.content_text:
A useful kitchen quote prices a defined scope. Compare cabinet layout, materials, hardware, installation and separate trade work before comparing the total.

Compare the same cabinet scope: A door refresh, replacement cabinets and a changed room layout are different projects. List what remains and what is removed, the number and arrangement of cabinets, drawers and panels, and the installation work required. A total without this detail cannot show whether two quotes cover the same outcome. There is no reliable project price until the scope and conditions are understood.

Separate the main quote factors: Cabinet size and complexity, substrate, visible finish, edging, drawer and hinge systems, internal accessories and appliance integration all affect the cabinetry scope. Transport, access, removal, protection and making-good also need an allocation. Benchtops, splashbacks, electrical and plumbing work should be identified as included, excluded or separately quoted rather than assumed to sit inside a cabinet total.

Keep the useful layout before cutting features: Retaining a workable cabinet layout or sound cabinet boxes may reduce the work, but their condition and compatibility need checking. Compare simpler door details, a different finish or fewer specialist accessories against daily storage needs. Moving services needs a separately defined trade scope; it cannot be priced from a universal allowance or justified by a generic saving claim.

Confirm lawful materials before ordering: Discuss the selected benchtop product with the responsible supplier and installer before specifying it. The engineered-stone prohibition and the distinction between new products and legacy work are explained in the sourced FAQ below. A material choice should be lawful, suitable for the room and coordinated with cabinet support and templating; it does not imply MEL ONE supplies or installs every benchtop system.

Decide what must stay and what can move: Keeping plumbing, waste and major electrical points can simplify a renovation, but it should not override a layout that fails the household. Start with the non-negotiables: cooking workflow, storage, access, appliance positions and circulation. Then identify which changes add genuine daily value and which are aesthetic moves that can be deferred or achieved another way.

Specify the joinery before selecting finishes: Cabinet depth, drawer configuration, appliance clearances, door style, handle detail and internal storage affect both cost and usability. Finish samples are important, but they should follow a layout that works. A client who understands the cabinet construction and hardware choices can compare alternatives more clearly than one choosing colour first and discovering functional compromises later.

Plan the trade sequence: A kitchen renovation often involves demolition, rough-in services, wall and floor preparation, cabinetry installation, benchtop templating, splashback work, appliance connection and final adjustment. The exact order depends on the project. Identifying who owns each handover helps prevent a finished cabinet being removed or altered because a service or surface was not ready.

Bring a brief, then resolve the missing selections: Start with the kitchen location, what you want to retain, storage priorities, appliance models if selected, and any known access or occupancy limits. Existing photos, approximate dimensions and drawings are optional at first enquiry. The site measure and agreed specification turn that initial discussion into a defined cabinetry quote; unresolved selections should remain identifiable allowances or exclusions.

items.title: Heritage timber restoration: principles before replacement
items.summary: Understand significance, retention and evidence when deciding how traditional timber work differs from ordinary renovation.
items.content_text:
Start with what gives the timber significance and what can safely be retained. Heritage restoration balances condition, use and the evidence of original construction before choosing a repair or replacement.

Check the property status and proposed change: Age or an architectural style alone does not establish heritage protection. Check the property’s status and discuss the proposed work through the relevant planning and heritage pathway before changing significant fabric. Approval requirements depend on the place and the work; there is no universal permit or mandatory adviser rule that can be inferred from a timber repair description. Official guidance is linked in the FAQ below.

Match the important detail, not an assumed period recipe: Surviving profiles, joints, hardware and finish evidence help establish an appropriate detail. A traditional joint or particular species may be relevant, but the repair specification should follow the actual element and the agreed conservation approach. Do not assume every period building needs the same timber, connector or coating simply because its appearance is similar.

Separate conservation advice from the carpentry scope: MEL ONE can discuss heritage timber carpentry against the recorded condition and agreed project information. The relevant authority decides formal approvals; heritage advisers and other responsible specialists address their own scopes. Ask what assessment, drawings, specifications and authorisations the proposed work needs before appointing the repair work.

Start with significance, condition and use: Heritage timber work is strongest when three questions are considered together: what is significant about the existing fabric, what condition is it in, and what does the building need to do today? A visible original window may have heritage value even when it needs careful repair for weathering or operation. The answer is rarely a simple choice between untouched and replaced.

Use evidence before making a replica: Profiles, surviving sections, old photographs, hardware and adjacent examples can all inform a repair or replacement detail. Recording these references before dismantling helps avoid a generic modern interpretation. Where a precise match is not possible, the proposed difference should be discussed openly with the project team and any relevant heritage adviser, not concealed by vague language.

Plan moisture management as part of restoration: Timber does not fail in isolation. Flashing, drainage, glazing, paint, sealants, ventilation and adjacent masonry can all influence the service life of a repaired element. A restoration scope should identify these interfaces and the trades involved. This protects both the historic material that remains and the new timber introduced as part of a careful repair.

Identify specialist interfaces before work starts: Structural concerns, active water entry, glazing, suspect coatings and other old materials may need separate assessment and specialist arrangements. Include those responsibilities in the project brief. A carpentry discussion does not establish engineering, hazardous-material or approval authority, and preparation should not disturb unknown materials merely to obtain a photograph.

Create a maintainable handover record: Keep photos, notes on retained and replaced elements, material or finish information, and a simple schedule for review. This record gives future owners or trades a clearer picture of what was repaired and why. Heritage stewardship is easier when maintenance is based on evidence rather than a cycle of reacting only after paint failure, water entry or decay becomes obvious.

items.title: Solid vs engineered timber flooring: choosing and restoring a floor
items.summary: Compare solid and engineered timber by product, subfloor, wear layer and maintenance, then decide what can be repaired or refinished.
items.content_text:
Neither solid nor engineered timber is automatically the better floor. Compare the selected product with the subfloor, moisture conditions, room use and future maintenance before choosing replacement or restoration.

Solid timber: assess thickness and existing condition: Solid timber boards have timber through their thickness, but that does not promise an unlimited number of sandings or a fixed lifespan. Existing sanding, fixing position, damage, movement and the board profile affect what can be restored. Assess the actual floor before treating sanding and oiling as the solution; local repairs or a different finish approach may be needed.

Engineered timber: compare the complete product: Engineered flooring combines a timber surface with a layered construction. Products differ in wear-layer thickness, installation method, finish and repair options. Price and suitability cannot be expressed as one percentage of solid flooring. Check the manufacturer’s information and the existing floor before assuming it can be sanded or installed directly over a particular slab.

Choose by room conditions and product requirements: A ground-floor slab does not automatically make engineered timber suitable, and an upper floor does not automatically favour solid timber. Moisture assessment, subfloor preparation, acoustic requirements, floor height and the selected system need to agree. For rooms with frequent water exposure, confirm the product’s stated application limits before choosing any floor covering.

Read the existing floor and subfloor first: A flooring choice is only as sound as the surface beneath it. Before selecting solid or engineered timber, understand slab or subfloor condition, flatness, moisture history, access, acoustic expectations and transitions to adjacent rooms. These factors affect preparation, installation method and long-term movement more than a showroom sample can reveal.

Choose for the room, not the trend: A sunny living room, upper-level bedroom, entry, apartment and renovation over an existing slab place different demands on timber flooring. Consider traffic, pets, direct light, furniture, cleaning habits and the desired feel underfoot. The most suitable product is the one whose visual character, maintenance needs and installation conditions all match the room’s real use.

Understand movement and visual variation: Timber is a natural material and can show grain, tone and seasonal movement. Board direction, width, feature grade, finish sheen and transition details influence how that variation reads across a room. Discussing samples and laying patterns early helps clients choose a look they will value over time rather than expecting every board to be identical.

Plan edges, stairs and adjoining finishes: Flooring projects often become complicated at thresholds, fireplace surrounds, built-ins, stair nosings, skirtings and door clearances. These details deserve attention before the main field is installed. A clear plan for edges and transitions creates a more durable, finished result and prevents a small unresolved junction from holding up a larger room at the end.

Care after installation: The right cleaning method, furniture protection, prompt attention to spills and sensible use of mats can help preserve a timber floor. Care advice should match the selected product and finish, not rely on a generic rule. Ask what to avoid, how to treat minor wear and when a professional review is appropriate so maintenance becomes planned rather than reactive.

items.title: Commercial carpentry fitout: sequence, scope and responsibilities
items.summary: Plan the timber part of a commercial fitout with clear drawings, site readiness, specialist interfaces and a recorded handover.
items.content_text:
Plan a commercial carpentry fitout around decisions and site readiness, then agree a programme. Design, approvals, services, manufacturing and installation depend on each other; a generic week count cannot establish your opening date.

Define the timber package and decision owners: Identify counters, fitted storage, trims, partitions or feature joinery that belong in the timber package. Name the owner or authorised tenant contact, designer, head contractor and responsible specialists where involved. Agree who supplies the drawings, coordinates services and authorises changes; do not assume a carpentry contractor also owns the entire tenancy design or approval process.

Release production after the required checks: Review site dimensions, finished floor levels, service positions, materials and approved drawings before the affected pieces are manufactured. Record what must be ready for installation, who provides access and where materials can be stored. Production and installation timing depend on those decisions and supplier availability, so confirm the programme against the actual scope.

Agree the carpentry handover and wider opening tasks: Check the installed timber work against approved drawings and the agreed scope, operate doors and drawers, record adjustments and supply selected product care information. The tenant, head contractor and responsible specialists still need to coordinate their own completion and opening requirements. A carpentry handover alone does not establish permission to open the premises.

Build the programme around dependencies: List unresolved approvals, selections, lead times, base-building preparation and service interfaces before fixing work dates. For an operating site, agree working areas, isolation, protection, deliveries and access arrangements. Ask who updates the programme when a dependency changes and how variations are authorised. Separate the desired opening date from the installation commitments actually agreed.

Confirm the base building information: Before a fitout programme is treated as fixed, confirm the lease or landlord requirements, existing services, base-build condition, access rules and the approvals pathway. A beautiful concept can still stall if the site cannot receive materials, a service route is unavailable or a required approval has not been allowed for. Early information protects the opening date.

Coordinate joinery with services: Counters, ceilings, partitions and feature walls commonly meet power, data, mechanical, hydraulic and fire services. The fitout team needs a shared view of where those interfaces occur and when they are checked. This is why shop drawings, site dimensions and trade coordination matter: they turn a visual layout into a buildable one without last-minute cutting into finished work.

Separate critical path from nice-to-have items: Some decisions affect every following trade: layout, approvals, long-lead materials, services and core joinery dimensions. Others—such as movable furniture or minor decorative items—can often be resolved later. Identifying the critical path helps owners direct their attention where it has the greatest program value and reduces the chance that a late aesthetic choice delays essential construction.

Protect quality under programme pressure: A fast commercial programme should not mean hiding decisions. Confirm finishes, access, tolerance, protection and handover responsibilities in writing, then review work at practical hold points. Clear records and a single point of contact make it easier to resolve issues while materials and trades are on site, rather than discovering them during final cleaning or the first week of trading.

Prepare an opening-focused brief: Tell MEL ONE the premises, intended opening date, occupancy arrangements, timber items and nominated project contacts. Existing drawings, dimensions and photos are optional for the initial enquiry. A site assessment can clarify the accessible conditions and carpentry scope. Required decisions and authorisations must be resolved by the responsible parties before the affected work proceeds.

items.title: Adelaide Carpentry Costs: How to Compare Rates and Written Quotes
items.summary: Understand carpentry labour and materials, photo estimates, hourly work and written quote inclusions before comparing Adelaide repair or installation proposals.
items.content_text:
A useful carpentry price starts with a defined job. This guide explains what to ask when comparing carpenter rates in Adelaide, so the price can be read alongside the work it covers.

Start with the scope rather than an advertised rate: If you are searching for a carpenter hourly rate in Adelaide, first write down the task, location and result you need. Adjusting a sticking door, replacing exposed deck boards and repairing concealed framing involve different preparation and uncertainty. MEL ONE's actual rates and project prices are not supplied in this guide; request pricing for your scope. A headline hourly figure cannot tell you the total without the expected time, materials, other charges and boundaries of the work. State whether you want a repair, replacement or assessment before choosing between proposals.

Separate a photo estimate from an assessed written quote: Photos can help explain a concern and support an initial discussion, but they cannot reveal every connection or concealed surface. A close image of a rotten sill may omit the adjoining frame, drainage problem or access needed to remove it. Ask which observations support an estimate, which assumptions remain and what inspection is needed before a written quote. Record the accessible areas assessed and whether opening up is included. Avoid treating a preliminary allowance as confirmation that the whole assembly is sound or that further work will be covered by the same amount.

Compare fixed scope pricing with hourly work: A fixed quote and hourly arrangement answer different questions. A quoted amount needs a defined scope, quantities, inclusions, exclusions and stated assumptions. For hourly work, ask how time is recorded, which activities are chargeable and how progress and further authorisation will be discussed. Clarify whether procurement, travel, setup and return visits form part of that time or are separate items. Neither arrangement removes uncertainty in hidden timber. Agree how investigation and any later repair will be priced rather than assuming every job can receive an unconditional fixed price before assessment.

Make labour, materials and procurement responsibilities visible: A carpentry quote in Adelaide should identify the elements to be repaired or supplied, with quantities or dimensions where practical. Describe the material, profile, grade or product selection rather than writing only 'new timber'. Confirm who orders, transports and stores it, and whether fittings, fasteners, protective coatings and delivery are included. Where you supply materials, discuss suitability, quantity and readiness before booking installation. Ask how unavailable products or requested substitutions will be handled. A material allowance needs a clear basis so a later selection can be compared with what was originally priced.

Check access, removal and the finished result: Work above a verandah, beneath a floor or around occupied rooms may need different access and protection arrangements. Identify restricted parking, stairs, working height, furniture, business hours and any coordination with other trades. Separate removal of old components from disposal, waste transport and final cleaning. State whether painting, staining, sealing, making good and adjoining surfaces are included, excluded or handled by another trade. For fascia, eaves or weatherboards, clarify the interfaces with gutters and surrounding materials. These details explain scope differences that a single total or hourly rate leaves hidden.

Read two deck repair quotes against the same brief: Suppose one proposal replaces selected deck boards while another allows for lifting a larger area and inspecting the joists. Their totals describe different work. Compare the measured area and board quantities, material specification, frame investigation, connections, stairs and balustrades. Then compare labour, procurement, access, removal, waste and finishing responsibilities. Ask both providers to identify retained components and unresolved findings against the same brief. An apparently lower price may cover fewer elements; a larger scope still needs explanation. Keep the comparison focused on what your deck needs rather than assuming either total proves better value.

Agree how hidden damage and variations will be handled: Opening a board, lining or joint can expose decay beyond the visible patch. That discovery can change the quantity of timber, connection details and specialist input needed. Ask how findings will be documented and which part of the original scope can proceed. MEL ONE confirms proposed scope changes and pricing for your approval before additional work proceeds. Record the agreed variation and any effect on timing. Where the damage affects load-bearing timber, resolve the required assessment and design responsibilities before treating it as a routine cosmetic repair.

Confirm the total and the terms before accepting: Read the quote as a complete document: agreed work, exclusions, allowances, GST treatment, payment stages, quote validity and proposed timing should be clear. Ask whether assessment, travel or a minimum booking charge applies; this guide does not assume those items are free or specify amounts. Note the acceptance process and who can approve changes, especially for rental or shared property. Send questions together so the revised written scope answers them before work starts. Keep the accepted quote and approved variations available for the final handover and account discussion.

items.title: Outdoor Timber Selection in Adelaide: Match Materials to the Site
items.summary: Prepare an outdoor material brief covering exposure, solid timber and composite options, framing compatibility, drainage, fixings, finishes and maintenance.
items.content_text:
Useful decking material advice in Adelaide starts with how the site is exposed and how the space will be used. A colour sample is one decision; the supporting structure, fixing system and maintenance plan need attention too.

Describe the exposure at the actual work area: Start with observations: which parts receive direct sun, stay shaded, collect leaves or remain wet after rain? Is sea air reaching the deck, or is the proposed work sheltered behind another building? Record irrigation, nearby planting, ground levels and water flowing from roofs or adjoining paving. Site specific timber selection needs this information rather than a suburb name alone. If you have an exposed coastal deck, report corroded fixings and where they occur as questions for assessment. Do not assume that changing the visible boards resolves the condition of the frame beneath them.

Compare solid timber and composite as complete systems: Compare the exact proposed products, their appearance, maintenance instructions and installation requirements. A preference for solid timber or composite does not establish that either can simply replace existing boards on the same supports. Ask the supplier or manufacturer to confirm the proposed supporting arrangement, fixing method and movement provisions for the selected product. ModWood publishes product installation and technical documents, illustrating why a composite board should be considered with its specified system. Product references are planning resources, not a claim that MEL ONE has installed or endorses that product.

Give the material specification enough detail: Ask the proposed supplier to identify the timber species or product name, dimensions, grade, treatment where relevant and intended use. Keep the board surface separate from the structural timber specification. Request supporting product information and flag any gaps for review by the responsible designer or supplier. Compare samples for appearance, but record what the order actually includes: profiles, edge details, colour selection and any coating. Avoid choosing solely from a species name or a general 'outdoor suitable' description. The brief should make substitutions visible before materials are purchased.

Plan drainage and ventilation before closing the edges: WoodSolutions' domestic deck guidance identifies drainage and ventilation as design considerations. Raise questions about water leaving the surface, air moving beneath the deck and access for inspection. Proposed edge screens, landscaping and storage beneath the boards should be included in that discussion. Ask the designer to resolve ground clearance, board spacing and interfaces using the selected system's requirements. These details are especially useful when comparing a raised deck with a constrained, low-level area. A decorative finish cannot stand in for a workable drainage and ventilation arrangement.

Check fixings, connections and the frame together: For exposed coastal timber work, WoodSolutions' guidance gives particular attention to fixing selection. Ask which fasteners and connectors are proposed for the actual exposure, timber and supporting material, and what documentation supports that choice. Identify mixed metals, existing corrosion and concealed connections as assessment questions. Board screws, clips, joist connections and post connections have different roles; replacing one visible fixing does not confirm the others are suitable. Record who will assess retained supports and resolve any required structural details before agreeing to a surface-only replacement.

Choose a finish with a realistic care plan: Decide how you want the surface to look and what upkeep you can accommodate. Ask the coating supplier about preparation, compatibility with existing finishes, end-grain treatment and the process for later refinishing. For composite, obtain the selected manufacturer's cleaning and care instructions; ModWood provides separate care resources in its technical documentation. Keep a record of the installed product and any finish so future cleaning or repair can follow the relevant guidance. Agree inspection and maintenance tasks for the individual site rather than assuming all outdoor boards follow one repainting or re-oiling timetable.

Resolve site constraints before committing to a material: Provide the property address and describe whether the proposal changes the structure, footprint, height or use of the outdoor area. Ask the relevant authority or responsible professional to assess applicable planning, building, heritage or bushfire-related requirements before final selection. For a proposed deck at an Adelaide Hills property, treat address-specific constraints as an early assessment question; a regional label does not determine a product's suitability. Where a ramp or threshold is involved, bring the user's access needs into the design discussion as well. This guide does not determine approval or compliance for a property.

Bring the material decision into the written scope: A useful brief names the intended use, observed exposure, proposed boards, supports, fixings, finish and maintenance expectations, then identifies decisions still awaiting assessment. Include access, removal of existing material, waste and any adjacent cladding or eaves repairs so the work can be coordinated. For restoration, ask which sound components could remain and what would be inspected before reuse. For a new outdoor structure, resolve drawings and responsibility for connections first. Record product documents and agreed substitutions with the quote so the chosen appearance and construction scope stay connected.

items.title: Adelaide Deck Replacement: When Boards, Joists or Fixings Need Attention
items.summary: A practical Adelaide deck replacement guide: how to distinguish surface wear from structural issues, what to inspect before requesting a quote, and how to scope a safer long-term repair.
items.content_text:
Surface wear can suit restoration, while decay, movement or damaged connections call for assessment before deciding on repair or replacement. Keep people away from an area that appears unsafe and describe the symptoms to the assessor.

Separate surface wear from a structural concern: Faded colour, raised grain and worn finish do not by themselves establish that the deck frame needs replacing. Movement, soft timber, loose connections or a damaged stair or balustrade need an assessment of the affected construction. Record what you can see safely from normal access; do not remove boards, load-test the deck or disturb supports to investigate it yourself.

How Adelaide exposure affects maintenance priorities: Sun, rain and coastal air do not affect every Adelaide deck in the same way. An exposed western deck may need a different finishing cycle from a sheltered courtyard, while salt-laden air can accelerate corrosion where the wrong fixings have been used. The useful starting point is not a generic lifespan claim: note the deck orientation, shade, moisture paths, proximity to the coast and whether leaf litter or planter boxes keep sections damp.

Prepare a quote-ready scope: Tell MEL ONE the deck location, preferred material, access constraints and whether you want the existing frame checked for reuse. Existing wide photos, close-ups and plans are optional; email them to handymanfelix.au2026@outlook.com if available. We inspect the frame, measure the deck and check stairs, balustrades, seating and posts. The quote separates demolition, structural repairs, boards, stairs, handrails, finishing and waste removal, with any site-dependent items explained.

Choose the next step based on evidence: MEL ONE inspects the deck boards, frame, post bases and connections on site to identify the repair required. We explain whether selective board replacement or a wider repair suits the condition, discuss approvals and engineering requirements, and confirm the work scope and quote before structural changes begin.

Ask for an assessment beyond the boards: The assessor needs to consider the accessible supports, framing, connections and moisture paths, not only the visible walking surface. Limited access may leave some conditions unresolved until an agreed investigation stage. The quote should identify those limits and explain how any newly exposed damage will be recorded and authorised before further work proceeds.

Material choices after removal: Once the existing construction is understood, the replacement decision can be specific: retain sound framing, replace damaged members, choose a board profile, resolve edge details and confirm how stairs or balustrades meet the new work. Comparing options against exposure, maintenance preference and intended use is more useful than selecting timber only by colour.

Avoid the common repair shortcuts: Covering decayed timber, tightening a loose board without finding the cause, or applying a fresh coating to a damp surface may improve appearance briefly without solving the condition below. A transparent scope identifies unknown areas, access limitations and the sequence for opening or repairing them, so the client can make an informed decision about risk and budget.

Coordinate stairs, balustrades and adjacent work: Deck replacement often touches more than boards. Stairs, privacy screens, roof posts, planters, lighting, pools and external doors can affect the workable sequence. Mapping these interfaces before demolition helps preserve access and avoids a new deck being held up by an overlooked connection, service or finish that belongs to another part of the project.

Questions to ask at handover: Ask which members were retained or replaced, what finish has been applied, how water is intended to drain, what areas need periodic review and how to report a concern. Keeping photographs of the work before boards are closed over can also be useful for future maintenance. Clear handover information is part of a durable deck, not an optional extra.

items.title: Adelaide Custom Wardrobe Planning: How to Measure, Specify and Avoid Storage Dead Space
items.summary: Plan a custom wardrobe for an Adelaide home with a practical checklist for measurements, internal storage, doors, materials and installation access before final design and pricing.
items.content_text:
MEL ONE turns your Adelaide custom wardrobe brief into a measured layout, an agreed materials and hardware specification, and a clear installation quote. Start with how you use the space, then confirm the site details before manufacture.

Measure the room, then measure the obstructions: Overall width, height and depth are only the first layer. Note skirtings, cornices, power points, windows, light switches, return walls and door swings, plus any variation in floor or wall level. In older Adelaide homes, walls and ceilings are not always square; an on-site measure before manufacture is the point at which the cabinet dimensions, filler panels and scribe details can be finalised.

Turn daily habits into internal zones: List what the wardrobe must hold before selecting finishes. Long-hang clothing, folded garments, shoes, linen, bags, drawers and seasonal storage each need different clearances. A useful layout normally mixes adjustable shelves with dedicated hanging zones and avoids deep, unlit shelves that become dead space. Consider who uses each side of the wardrobe and whether future changes—such as a child growing or a room changing function—are likely.

Select doors and materials for the room, not the showroom: Hinged doors need clear swing space; sliding doors preserve circulation but limit access to part of the interior at once. Mirrored, painted and timber-look finishes each change light, maintenance and the visual weight of the room. For wardrobes near bathrooms, laundries or external walls, discuss moisture exposure and ventilation so the substrate, edging and installation detail suit the location.

Plan the installation as carefully as the cabinet: Confirm access from the street to the room, stair turns, parking, flooring protection and the timing of painting, electrical work and new carpet. A clear installation sequence reduces the risk that joinery is measured before adjoining finishes are ready. To request a quote, tell MEL ONE what the wardrobe needs to store and the finishes you prefer. Existing room photos, a rough sketch and approximate measurements are optional; email them to handymanfelix.au2026@outlook.com if available. MEL ONE confirms the room and access measurements on site.

Set realistic depths and clearances: The internal depth, drawer projection, hanging clearance and shelf spacing must work with the garments and room, not just fit a nominal cabinet size. A wardrobe can lose useful capacity when a door, bed or window restricts access. Discussing these constraints early allows the layout to favour the items used daily and reserve higher or deeper areas for occasional storage.

Use light, power and ventilation deliberately: Integrated lighting, power points and ventilation can make a wardrobe easier to use, but they need to be planned before the unit is built. Identify what requires electrical coordination, where cables or drivers can be accessed and whether exterior walls or adjoining wet areas create condensation concerns. These interfaces are resolved with the appropriate trades rather than retrofitted blindly.

Understand visible finish and tolerance: Filler panels, scribes and small shadow lines are often the practical way for cabinetry to meet existing walls that are not straight. They should be treated as considered details, not defects. Reviewing samples, handle positions and the intended reveal between doors gives everyone a shared expectation before a custom wardrobe is manufactured and installed.

Plan for changing needs: A well-planned wardrobe can adapt when a child's room changes, a guest room becomes a study or a household's storage mix evolves. Adjustable shelves, removable rails and sensible drawer sizing can offer flexibility without making the interior feel generic. The right choices depend on the client’s likely use, rather than adding every accessory available.

Review before final sign-off: At completion, check door movement, drawer operation, alignment, visible edges, hardware and the way the unit meets the floor, wall and ceiling. Keep care information for the selected surface and note any access points for lighting or services. A brief practical review lets small adjustments be identified while the installation team and materials are still available.

From your first brief to an agreed wardrobe scope: Start with a storage list and the door or finish options you want. Existing room photos and approximate dimensions are optional; email them to handymanfelix.au2026@outlook.com if available. MEL ONE then carries out the site measure, checks walls, floors and access, and confirms the proposed internal layout. Review door movement, drawer projection, hardware clearances, filler details and any lighting interfaces together. Approve the drawings and specification before the final quoted scope proceeds to manufacture and installation.

What your wardrobe quote should include: The quote should describe the wardrobe location, layout and quantities: hanging zones, shelves, drawers and any selected accessories. Identify the cabinet substrate, edging, visible finishes, door material, handles and hardware. Confirm whether removal of an existing unit, transport, floor and room protection, waste removal, installation, wall or trim making-good, and lighting interfaces are included. Record exclusions and responsibilities clearly so the total scope is easy to compare.

Keep a budget estimate separate from the confirmed quote: An early budget estimate uses the information and selections available at that stage. A confirmed quote follows the site measure and agreed layout, materials, hardware and installation conditions. Where something still needs checking, record the assumption and how it will be resolved. Ask MEL ONE to explain the pricing basis and included costs rather than treating a photo-based estimate as an approved manufacturing specification.

Approve changes before manufacture or installation: Adding drawers, changing hinged doors to sliding doors or selecting a different door material can change hardware, internal access, fabrication and installation work. MEL ONE records the revised layout or specification and explains the effect on price and scheduling in a written variation. Approve that change before the affected work proceeds; keep the approved version alongside the original quote.

Complete a practical wardrobe handover: At handover, compare the installed layout and visible finish with the approved scope. Operate the doors and drawers, check handles, alignment, shelving and agreed lighting access, and record any adjustments or outstanding work. Keep the surface-care information and final specification with the completion record. This gives the household a useful reference for routine care and future changes.

items.title: Adelaide heritage timber repairs: prepare a condition record and scope
items.summary: Prepare an element-by-element condition record, access notes and repair questions for heritage doors, windows and external timber.
items.content_text:
Prepare a condition record before deciding the repair scope: identify each element, describe visible symptoms and note access and existing project advice. This practical brief follows the conservation principles explained in the companion heritage guide.

Give each timber element a clear reference: Use a room, elevation or simple element name such as front window or side door so everyone discusses the same item. Note sticking, visible decay, water entry, damaged profiles or missing hardware from safe normal access. Existing photos are optional for the first enquiry; do not disturb coatings, glazing or timber to make a record. The site assessment provides the accessible condition detail needed to develop the scope.

Record the repair decision for each element: Ask the proposed scope to identify retained material, local repairs, replicated components or replacement items and the evidence behind each decision. Include profile references, finish responsibilities and unresolved conditions. The method must suit the assessed element and agreed conservation approach; a photo or generic repair description is not a specification for cutting or rebuilding old timber.

Attach known heritage and approval information: Include any known listing status, previous advice, approved drawings and relevant correspondence with the project record. Requirements depend on the place and proposal; use PlanSA guidance to start the approval check and ask the relevant authority about unresolved requirements. MEL ONE’s carpentry scope should follow the agreed project information rather than promise the authority’s decision.

Give the repair a maintenance plan: Timber lasts longer when paint failure, failed sealant, blocked drainage paths and exposed end grain are addressed early. At handover, ask what has been repaired, which finish system has been used, when it should be reviewed and which warning signs—such as cracking, sticking, water entry or soft timber—should prompt another inspection.

Record moisture symptoms and responsibility: Note when water entry occurs, which areas remain damp and any previous repairs. Accessible observations help the assessment, but hidden drainage, flashing, glazing or wall problems may need another specialist. Ask who investigates the cause and what must be resolved before the timber repair is finished; replacement timber alone does not establish that water entry has been fixed.

Respect evidence of the original construction: Old hardware, profiles, glazing bars, joints and paint layers can help explain how an element was built and what makes it visually significant. Recording those details before removal creates a better basis for repair or replication. It also allows owners, designers and heritage advisers to discuss a proposed change using evidence rather than a guess based on a modern equivalent.

Scope concealed-condition risk honestly: External joinery can conceal deterioration behind paint, trims or internal linings. MEL ONE checks the accessible timber on site and agrees any careful opening-up needed to identify the damage. If hidden decay is found, we explain the additional repair and agree the scope and quote with you before proceeding.

Coordinate paint, glazing and hardware: A repaired timber window or door depends on more than its joinery. Glazing, putty or sealant, hardware adjustment, paint preparation and final coating need to follow an appropriate sequence. Clarifying those interfaces early prevents a repaired sash or door from being installed without the finishing work required to protect it from weather and daily use.

Build a staged restoration plan: For a larger Adelaide property, the best route may be to prioritise the most exposed or unsafe openings first, then schedule the remaining work over time. A condition record, photo set and agreed repair approach make that staging more consistent. It helps owners protect important fabric while planning budgets, approvals and access in a calm, evidence-led way.
